steps.instruction:
(Protocol)Aggregating expert-elicited data for prediction: A scoping review of
statistical methods, experiments, and applications
Thomas McAndrew, Ph.D, 1, ⇤ Nutcha Wattanachit,1 Casey Gibson, 1 and Nicholas G. Reich, Ph.D 1, †
1Department of Biostatistics and Epidemiology, School of Public Health and Health
Sciences, University of Massachusetts, Amherst, Massachusetts, United States of America
(Dated: October 2, 2019)
Combining forecasts from experts, compared to a statistical model, is often more accurate when
data is sparse or prone to revision. Mathematical approaches for combining forecasts span several
disciplines. Economics, marketing, population dynamics, and politics all rely on expert intuition to
make predictions about the future. Because expert-elicited combination forecasting is spread across
di↵erent domains, researchers use a diverse set of deﬁnitions to describe the same concepts. The
diversity of applications also means methodological approaches are developed in parallel rather than
building on one another. Our scoping review aims to unify these varied deﬁnitions and method-
ological approaches, map key terminology, and summarize applications of combination forecasting,
experimental designs, and methods to mathematically aggregate expert-elicited data.
We will collect articles related to methods for aggregating expert-elicited forecasts from the Web
of Science database. An article is deﬁned as in-scope if it describes eliciting expert judgments and
combining them to make a prediction about a natural phenomena or future event. Articles will be
considered in-scope if two committee members read the article and agree it meets the above criteria.
From the ﬁnal set of in-scope articles, we will extract: the application, experimental design,
metrics used to compare forecasts, and the mathematical model used to combine forecasts. Common
terminology will be consolidated and discussed. We will also ask of each article a pre-speciﬁed set
of questions related to combination forecasting.
This protocol prespeciﬁes all criteria and steps for conducting a scoping review on methods for
aggregating expert-elicited predictions. All aspects of this protocol were reviewed and agreed on by
the coauthors, and any signiﬁcant deviations from this protocol will be recorded and an amended
protocol submitted. This scoping review—selecting articles in a rigorous, prespeciﬁed, and unbiased
way—aims to map, classify, and summarize all aspects of literature that aggregates expert-elicited
predictions.
I. SIGNA TURE P AGE
Thomas McAndrew
Nutcha Wattanachit
G. Casey Gibson
Nicholas G. Reich
⇤ mcandrew@umass.edu
† nick@schoolph.umass.edu
II. BACKGROUND
Accurate forecasts depend on collecting data related to
the target of interest. When data is sparse, or prone to
revision, statistical models can struggle to make accurate
forecasts of the future. Human judgment is not subject
to the same restrictions as statistical models. We can
draw on unstructured data, reason about whether past
data is predictive of the future, and build complex models
of the associations between phenomena. A model com-
bining expert predictions is an attempt to collect this
unstructured data and intuition and produce a forecast
representing experts’ collective knowledge.
This scoping review will map how expert predictions
are combined to produce aggregate forecasts. Included
articles must have solicited at least two expert human
forecasts, and use a mathematical method of aggregating
forecasts. Our scoping review will produce simple and
concrete deﬁnitions, identify approaches to aggregation,
experimental designs used to test forecasting model, and
expose gaps in the current literature.
In what follows, we describe our scoping review ap-
proach. We state our objectives, research question,
search strategy, and analysis. This protocol is meant
to maintain a rigorous and unbiased strategy for better
understanding approaches to combining expert data.

2
III. OBJECTIVE
This scoping review’s primary objective is: mapping of
key terminology, summarizing applications, experimental
designs, and methods to aggregate expert-elicited predic-
tions.
III.1. Primary objectives
1. Map characteristics of aggregating expert data: the
timeframe, application, journals where literature is
published, methodological approaches, methods of
comparison, and experimental designs.
2. Condense a diverse set of terminology into a set of
succinct deﬁnitions
3. Identify gaps and future directions for this ﬁeld of
research
IV. METHODS
IV.1. Research Question
This scoping review asks “What statistical and quanti-
tative methods are used to aggregate expert-elicited pre-
dictions?”. The use of “statistical” and “quantitative”
requires scoped articles take a mathematical or statisti-
cal approach to learning from expert data. Articles in
scope must provide or reference sound statistical tech-
niques.
IV.2. Search strategy
Web of Science will be used to ﬁnd articles related
to combining expert-elicited predictions. We will use
the following search term: (expert* or human* or
crowd*) NEAR judgement AND (forecast* or
predict*) AND (combin* or assimilat*) and restrict
our search to English-language articles only.
Articles returned from the Web of Science search will
be randomly assigned to two reviewers. Each reviewer
will read the title and abstract, and determine if the ar-
ticle is in or out of scope. If both reviewers agree the
article is considered in scope. If the reviewers disagree,
the article will be assigned to a third reviewer to decide
if the article is in or out of scope. We will collect all in
scope article’s full text.
V. EXTRACTING INFORMA TION FROM FULL
TEXT AR TICLES
All in scope full texts will be randomly assigned to
a reviewer. The reviewer will read the article in full
and answer a set of prespeciﬁed questions (Table I). The
prespeciﬁed questions focus on the experimental design,
mathematical/statistical method, sample size, compari-
son metrics, and application area.
VI. ANAL YSIS
A ﬂow chart will be presented that counts the number
of articles returned from Web of Science, number of ar-
ticles after review, and number of ﬁnal in scope articles.
During full-text review, articles may be discovered unre-
lated to combining expert judgement data and an addi-
tional category will be added to the ﬂow-chart “Analysis
articles” that counts only those articles used for analysis.
Yes/No prespeciﬁed questions will be summarized by
frequencies and percentages. The total number of fore-
casts, and number of expert forecasts will be summarized
by mean and standard deviation. If the distribution is
skewed or has outliers, the median and IQR will be re-
ported. We will propose a single name that consolidates
di↵erent ways of referring to the same evaluation metric
and model used.
Special attention will be paid to type of model used
for aggregating judgements, quality of data judges are
thought to use for prediction, and whether or not the
model combines point or probability distributions.
VII. PLANS FOR UPDA TING THE REVIEW
If the coauthors decide to change the above protocol,
an amended protocol will be resubmitted before moving
forward and deciding on the ﬁnal list of included articles
for this scoping review. Additional amendments will be
labeled v1. X, the ﬁrst amendment labeled v1.1, second
amendment labeled v1.2, and so on.
VIII. ST A TEMENT OF CONFLICTS OF
INTEREST
All authors have no conﬂicts of interest.
